segments.text: Comparison of a high-flow humidified nasal cannula to nasal continuous positive airway pressure in children with acute bronchiolitis: experience in a pediatric intensive care unit
Prune Metge & Céline Grimaldi & Sophie Hassid &
Laurent Thomachot & Anderson Loundou & Claude Martin & Fabrice Michel
Received: 26 November 2013 /Revised: 6 January 2014 /Accepted: 22 January 2014 /Published online: 14 February 2014 # Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg 2014

Abstract The objective of the current study is to compare the use of a nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) to a high-flow humidified nasal cannula (HFNC) in infants with acute bronchiolitis, who were admitted to a pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) during two consecutive seasons. We retrospectively reviewed the medical records of all infants admitted to a PICU at a tertiary care French hospital during the bronchiolitis seasons of 2010/11 and 2011/12. Infants admitted to the PICU, who required noninvasive respiratory support, were included. The first noninvasive respiratory support modality was nCPAP during the 2010/11 season, while HFNC was used during the 2011/2012 season. We compared the length of stay (LOS) in the PICU; the daily measure of PCO2 and pH; and the mean of the five higher values of heart rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), FiO2, and SpO2 each day, during the first 5 days. Thirty-four children met the inclusion criteria: 19 during the first period (nCPAP group) and 15 during the second period (HFNC group). Parameters such as LOS in PICU and oxygenation were similar in the two groups. Oxygen weaning occurred during the same time for the two groups. There were no differences between the two groups for RR, HR, FiO2, and CO2 evolution. HFNC therapy failed in three patients, two of whom required invasive mechanical

Conclusion : We did not find a difference between HFNC and nCPAP in the management of severe bronchiolitis in our PICU. Larger prospective studies are required to confirm these findings.
Keywords Acute viral bronchiolitis . Respiratory distress . Nasal CPAP . High-flow nasal cannula

In acute viral bronchiolitis, distal airway obstruction reduces dynamic pulmonary compliance and increases the expiratory time, creating an intrinsically positive-end expiratory pressure [2, 7, 10]. In the most severe cases, respiratory failure occurs, associated with hypercapnia, hypoxia, and apneic syndrome. Hospitalization in the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) can therefore be required for respiratory support treatment [5].

Several studies have demonstrated the efficacy of nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP), by reducing the clinical signs of respiratory distress, the work of breathing, hypercapnia, the need for tracheal intubation as well as reducing complications of invasive ventilation [2, 5, 7, 8, 13, 17, 19].

Recently, high-flow humidified nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy has been tested for the management of acute respiratory failure in adults and children [6, 9, 14]. It delivers heated, humidified gas with a constantly higher flow than a standard cannula. It allows constant FiO2 of inspired gas, washes out the dead space, and provides a variable level of positive airway pressure (depending on several parameters [6, 9]). Its use is rapidly growing in neonatal intensive care units (NICU), because it is easier, better tolerated, associated with less nasal trauma, and has a lower cost compared to that of the usual CPAP devices [4, 21]. Some authors have shown that its use in acute viral bronchiolitis management can also reduce respiratory rate (RR), PCO2, and intubation rate; however, failure of this treatment in the PICU could occur in more than 20 % of cases [1, 15].

Data comparing nCPAP to HFNC in infants with acute viral bronchiolitis are limited [12, 20]. In 2011, we transitioned from the use of nCPAP to HFNC as a noninvasive respiratory support in infants with acute bronchiolitis as well as acute respiratory failure, prior to use of invasive mechanical ventilation. As stated, the objective of the current study is to compare the use of nCPAP to HFNC as noninvasive respiratory support systems in infants with acute bronchiolitis admitted to the PICU during two consecutive seasons.
We conducted a retrospective study of infants admitted to our tertiary center ' s PICU during two consecutive seasons of acute bronchiolitis: the winters of 2010/11 and 2011/12.

The noninvasive respiratory support used during the 2010/11 season was nCPAP. In September 2011, we transitioned from nCPAP to HFNC as the modality of choice for noninvasive respiratory support in infants with acute bronchiolitis admitted to the PICU.
The ethics committee waived the need for consent in this retrospective review of medical records, which is congruent with French law.

Infants with acute bronchiolitis, and one of or more of the following, were eligible for inclusion in the study: (1) oxygen requirement to maintain SpO2>92 %, (2) hypercarbia PCO2> 50 mmHg, (3) acidosis pH<7.30, and (4) apnea. Infants who needed tracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation at the time of admission to the PICU, however, were excluded.

According to our guidelines during the first period (2010/11), infants needing respiratory support were initially treated with nCPAP (Infant Flow, Viasys Healthcare Inc., Yorba Linda, CA, USA). The positive airway pressure objective was 4 to 6 cm H2O. If failure did occur with this treatment, pressure support noninvasive ventilation or tracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation were initiated, according to the clinical judgment of the physician in charge. During the second period (2011/12), the protocol was modified and the initial respiratory support was replaced by HFNC, using a heated humidified high-flow delivery system (RT329 System with the MR850 humidifier, Fisher & Paykel Healthcare, Auckland, New Zealand) and connected to an oxygen therapy nasal cannula (BC2745 and BC2755, Fisher & Paykel Healthcare, Auckland, New Zealand). The nasal prong size was selected according to the manufacturer ' s recommendations, while the system was equipped with a pressure release valve set at 45 cm H2O.

Initial flow rate was set at 1 L/kg/min during the first hour, though, it could be increased by 1 L/kg/min (up to 3 L/kg/min without exceeding 8 L/min) if the initial clinical status did not improve, as per the physician in charge ' s evaluation of the patient. In the event of worsened clinical or blood gas parameters or a need for FiO2>40 %, despite maximal flow, HFNC was replaced by nCPAP and failure of treatment was considered. Similar to the first period, failure of nCPAP treatment was assessed by the physician in charge and could be switched for noninvasive mechanical ventilation or tracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation.

In both periods, monitoring included heart rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), and SpO2 continuous recording. HR, RR, SPO2, and FiO2 were noted every hour. Noninvasive arterial pressure was also measured every hour as well. Capillary blood gas analysis (RAPIDLab 1265, Siemens, Munich, Germany) was performed on admission, and then at a minimum of once a day, by heel puncture using capillary tubes. All infants had peripheral venous catheters with glucose infusion for the first day. Continuous enteral nutrition was introduced at 20 ml/kg/h by an orogastric tube on the first day, and then progressively increased.

Weaning from respiratory support was the same for both techniques and was started once the FiO2<25 % and the PCO2<45 mmHg. Respiratory support was replaced by lowflow nasal cannula (1 L/min). FiO2 was adapted to maintain SpO2>90 %. In the case of weaning failure (based on clinical judgment or SpO2<90 % with FiO2 100 %), noninvasive respiratory support was restarted and then stopped the next day.

The following information was extracted from the patient ' s medical records: age, gender, weight, location prior to PICU admission, positive or negative respiratory syncytial virus detected by PCR in nasal secretions, HR, RR, FiO2, pH, and PCO2 at admission. The mean of the five higher values of HR, RR, and FiO2 for each day and the first daily measure of pH and PCO2 were recorded for the first 5 days of PICU hospitalization. Data collection was stopped in the case of respiratory support treatment modification (a switch to CPAP when the infant was treated by HFNC or intubation when the infant was treated by nCPAP), which included respiratory support weaning. All treatment complications were also recorded.

Data are expressed as medians (25e -75e percentile) and percentages, with parametric statistics also employed. Comparisons between groups at the time of admission were assessed using Student ' s t test or chi-2 test. HR, RR, FiO2, and PCO2 evolutions were compared between the two groups with a two-way analysis of variance for repeated measures. The statistical analyses were performed with the SPSS software package version 17.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). Statistical significance was defined as p <0.05.

Thirty-four infants were included in the analysis: 19 for the first period (2010/11; nCPAP group), 15 for the second period (2011/12; HFNC group). Age, gender, weight at admission, RSV status, location prior to PICU admission, and hospital length of stay before PICU admission were similar between the two groups (Table 1).

Both groups were similar for pH, PCO2, and oxygen saturation at admission and for maximal HR, RR, and FiO2 during the first day in the PICU. Length of stay in the PICU was not statistically different between the two groups (Table 1). Two infants in the HFNC group had comorbidities: one had a history of severe prematurity (28 SA) with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), and the second had Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

Treatment failure occurred in one infant in the nCPAP group on day 2. He was intubated because of respiratory exhaustion, along with severe respiratory acidosis (pH 7.08, PCO2 76 mmHg), which was responsible for somnolence and global hypotonia. In the HFNC group, treatment failure occurred in three patients on day 2, so that treatment was switched to nCPAP. Clinical improvement was observed for one of them, while the two others required intubation and mechanical ventilation for less than 12 h after treatment modification.

Multivariate analysis for repeated measures showed a difference in evolution of the mean maximal HR from day 1 to day 5 in the two groups ( p <0.01), but there was no difference in HR between groups (Fig. 1).

Mean maximal RR decreased significantly in the two groups from day 1 to day 5 ( p <0.01), but there was no difference of the RR between the two groups (Fig. 1). PCO2 significantly decreased in both groups from day 1 to day 5 ( p <0.01), with a trend to lower values in the HFNC group, although the difference did not reach statistical significance ( p =0.051) (Fig. 1).

Mean maximal FiO2 decreased constantly in the two groups ( p <0.01) after use of noninvasive respiratory support, without a significant difference between groups. Oxygen weaning was accomplished during the same time for both groups (Fig. 2).
The mean pH significantly increased in the two groups over time ( p <0.001), without any difference observed between them (Fig. 1). No treatment complications were noted in the two groups.

We compared two groups of infants treated with nCPAP or HFNC for acute viral bronchiolitis in the PICU. We did not find any difference between groups for respiratory parameters or length of stay in the PICU, suggesting that HFNC is as efficient as nCPAP in improving respiratory distress in infants with acute bronchiolitis.

The two groups in our study were similar at the time of PICU admission. Pediatric index mortality 2 (PIM 2) and length of stay in the PICU are concordant with previous reports [2, 7, 15]. The management of acute viral bronchiolitis is well codified in our unit, and except for respiratory support, none of the treatments was added or modified between the two seasons. In particular, there was no need for nebulized bronchodilatator or corticosteroid treatment, and as such, we

believe that HFNC was as efficient as nCPAP. This result is in accordance with a recent randomized study, which also found no difference between the two devices in preventing reintubation in preterm neonates [3].

Similar to nCPAP, HFNC is known to provide positive-end expiratory pressure. In patients with moderate respiratory distress, due to acute viral bronchiolitis, HFNC with a flow of 2 L/kg/min develops a relevant pharyngeal pressure, thereby reducing respiratory effort by 50 % and improving clinical status [16]. In 18 preterm infants, using HFNC at 3, 4, and 5 L/ min flow allowed for decreased work of breathing as well as using nCPAP at 6 cm H2O pressure [18]. In our study, oxygenation parameters were identical in the two groups and improved in the same manner. Although the difference was not significant, we observed higher FiO2 in the HFNC group during the first 2 days, despite equal FiO 2 on admission. Three children in the HFNC group required a switch in treatment to nCPAP, and two were intubated. Clinical deterioration occurred in the first 24 h after admission, while intubation was performed on day 2. The positive-end expiratory pressure (PEEP) delivered with HFNC depends on the flow, diameter of the nasal prongs relative to the nostrils, and gas leaks by mouth. Therefore, PEEP level remains uncertain and possibly time-varying [11, 16], unlike the Instant Flow SiPAP system, which provides stable PEEP. This variability in PEEP level could be responsible for temporary alveolar derecruitment, leading to respiratory worsening.

Afavorable effect on hypercapnia was also observed in the two groups. This effect has been widely reported with nCPAP [2, 19], but only one study reported PCO2 improvement with HFNCinacute viral bronchiolitis [13]. Interestingly, we found a trend that lowers PCO2 in the HFNC group. One explanation for this is an important wash out of dead space with HFNC [6, 9]. Greater improvement could also be linked to better tolerance of HFNC. Indeed, nCPAP requires a hermetic nasal mask, which is difficult to install and maintain in place. It affects points of high pressure on the face and could be responsible for pain, discomfort, and at times cutaneous necrosis [3]. Resulting agitation can impair gas exchange, hence CO2 removal. Nonresponders to HFNC have recently been studied as well [1]. Higher PCO2 and lower RR on admission were associated with HFNC failure; however, in our two cases, these criteria were not present.

Several limitations of our study must be mentioned. The samples sizes are small, thus limiting the value of our findings, insofar as small variations cannot be shown. Apnea occurrence, clinical scores, and the exact conditions of nasal prong use are not available in a retrospective study. For example, use of a pacifier reduces mouth air leaks and could have impacted treatment efficiency [16]. Another problem was that treatment failure was not clearly defined, but left to the clinical judgment of the physician in charge. Finally, it is important to note that the population of this study was predominantly very young infants; as a result, the findings could not be extended to older children.

In this study comparing HFNC to nCPAP for severe acute viral bronchiolitis in infants, we observed no difference in the length of stay in the PICU, respiratory rate, PCO2, FiO2, and duration of oxygen support. These results should encourage further investigation in order to more comprehensively compare respiratory supports in a larger, controlled prospective evaluation.
